cim: N.J. lawmakers move to regulate AI in insurance, housing and the workplace
kihagyva: P3: 50 pont, tendencia 20%, jóváhagyás után fordul
cim_eredeti: N.J. lawmakers move to regulate AI in insurance, housing and the workplace
szoveg_eredeti:
New Jersey lawmakers are moving to regulate the growing use of artificial intelligence in insurance, housing and the workplace, advancing legislation intended to protect consumers and workers while drawing concerns from businesses about higher costs and restrictions on emerging technology.

The Assembly Science, Innovation and Technology Committee has taken up bills that would limit the use of AI in insurance claim denials, regulate automated tenant screening and impose new requirements on electronic monitoring of employees. Lawmakers are also considering measures to require greater transparency from data center developers, whose rapid expansion has raised concerns about electricity demand, land use and environmental impacts.

Assemblyman Chris Tully (D-Bergenfield), the committee’s chairman, said the legislation reflects the need to protect consumers as artificial intelligence becomes more widely used.

“As the Assembly Science, Innovation and Technology Committee continues to address the societal impacts of artificial intelligence,” Tully said, “today’s bills represent an important step forward. While AI systems can improve efficiency and tackle fraud, we must protect people from automatic denial by algorithms. When a major decision affects someone’s life, there must always be a human in the loop.”

“By mandating human oversight for these critical systems, we are establishing the common-sense guardrails necessary to use these powerful tools responsibly.”

But the proposals have encountered resistance from business groups and industry representatives who question whether lawmakers can effectively regulate technology that continues to evolve.

Assemblyman Chris DePhillips (R-Wyckoff) abstained on two bills dealing with insurance claims and tenant screening, saying he believed supporters and opponents could resolve their differences.

“I abstained on both of the bills because I felt that the proponents of the bills and the people who were testifying against them didn’t seem that far apart and I felt there was an opportunity for both sides to get together and collaborate,” he said.

One bill, A5494, would prohibit certain uses of artificial intelligence in denying homeowners, automobile and flood insurance claims. It advanced with DePhillips abstaining and every other committee member voting in favor.

Insurance industry representatives raised concerns that the restrictions could limit their ability to use new technology and leave companies at a competitive disadvantage.

Assemblywoman Carmen Morales (D-Bloomfield) defended the proposal as a consumer protection measure.

“This bill really is about transparency “

A second bill, A5495, would regulate the use of automated tenant screening systems to evaluate prospective renters. It also advanced with DePhillips abstaining and the remaining committee members voting in favor.

Assemblyman Balvir Singh (D-Burlington) acknowledged the difficulty of developing regulations for technology that is changing so quickly.

“Personally, I feel like I’m learning to ride a bike while riding it,” Singh said.

Nicholas Kikis, vice president of legislative and regulatory affairs for the New Jersey Apartment Association, did not take a position on the tenant screening bill but warned that artificial intelligence has made it increasingly difficult for landlords to detect fraudulent applications.

“We are seeing an increase in fraud that is being generated by artificial intelligence,” he said.

Kikis pointed to income verification as an example. Documents that landlords previously could verify with relative ease can now be altered using AI, making it harder to determine whether prospective tenants are providing accurate financial information. He questioned whether the legislation might also restrict landlords from using AI to detect the same kinds of fraud.

Jeff Kolekowski of the New Jersey Builders Association raised similar concerns without taking a formal position on the bill.

The committee also held a discussion-only hearing on A4981, which would regulate artificial intelligence-based electronic monitoring systems used in employment and public services.

Assembly members Heather Simmons (D-Glassboro) and Cody Miller (D-Monroe) are sponsoring the proposal, along with 16 other Democratic co-sponsors.

Business groups warned that the legislation could impose substantial costs and leave employers uncertain about which technologies would be covered.

Anthony Russo of the Commerce and Industry Association of New Jersey questioned the scope and expense of the proposed requirements.

“We don’t see this as an AI bill,” he said. “It’s going to add a high cost to companies that invent those technologies, and they’re gonna have to pay to have it approved”

“This thing goes through; you’re just adding to the cost of doing business,” Russo stated.

Jack Ramirez of the New Jersey Business and Industry Association said the bill’s definition of artificial intelligence was too broad and could subject ordinary business tools to additional regulation.

“One of our primary concerns is that this bill does not establish a sufficiently clear definition of artificial intelligence “

“Businesses are going to be left guessing about what technologies and tools are actually subject to these requirements,” he said further.

Labor representatives defended the legislation, arguing that employers should face restrictions on how they use artificial intelligence to monitor workers.

Eric Richards, legislative affairs coordinator for the New Jersey AFL-CIO, said the technology could dramatically change working conditions and threaten employee privacy.

“It’s clear artificial intelligence has the power to change the very nature of work as we know it”

“We’re not against AI ” We also know that without oversight, AI companies pose tremendous risk to working people, eliminating our jobs, eliminating our privacy.

Richards said the bill would establish protections without preventing employers from adopting new technology.

“The bill puts workers’ and working people’s issues front and center”

“This legislation puts clear common-sense ground rules for how AI can be used in the workplace”

“It makes sure your employer can’t spy on you when you’re off the clock “

The committee has also turned its attention to data centers, with lawmakers seeking to give local officials and residents more information about proposed developments before they move through the municipal approval process.

A5224 would require data center developers to disclose certain information to the public and elected officials before preliminary site plan consideration under the Municipal Land Use Law.

Another bill, S4304, sponsored by State Sens. Linda Greenstein (D-Plainsboro) and Brian Stack (D-Union City), would prohibit agreements intended to conceal certain information about data center developments. Its Assembly counterpart is A2774.

Greenstein, who testified before the committee, criticized the use of nondisclosure agreements that prevent communities from learning details about proposed projects.

“If you don’t play by the rules of open government, you don’t get to build in New Jersey “

“When you talk about the future of New Jersey, you can not ignore the rapid expansion of Digital infrastructure”

Greenstein said confidentiality agreements could prevent residents and local officials from learning the full extent of a project’s electricity demands and environmental effects.

“They use restrictive NDAs to conceal the massive scale, the staggering energy demands and the localized environmental impact “

Chris Sotiro of the Climate Revolution Action Network also criticized the agreements.

“These developers are not interested in transparency; they’re interested in hiding”

The Assembly version of the legislation, A2774, advanced with bipartisan support. DePhillips, the only Republican present at the hearing, voted in favor. Assemblyman Greg McGuckin (R-Toms River) was absent.
